UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
)

MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE LIMITED ANSWER,  
AND LIMITED ANSWER, OF  
EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC. 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 East 
Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC”) moves for leave to file this limited answer and 
answers the September 10, 2026 answer submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) in the 
above-captioned proceeding.2 EKPC’s Protest opposed PJM’s proposed revisions to its Open 
Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load 
Serving Entities in the PJM Region (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement 
(“RBP”) because the RBP Proposal is unjust and unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, inconsistent 
with the Commission’s cost-causation principles and the boundaries of federal and state 
jurisdiction, and contrary to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.3 PJM’s Answer does not resolve 
those defects. For the reasons set forth herein and in the EKPC Protest, EKPC respectfully requests 
that the Commission reject the RBP Proposal. 
EKPC also submits this Limited Answer to place PJM’s post-protest explanations and 
implementation materials in their proper context. PJM’s Answer relies on clarifications,

developments to assist the Commission in evaluating whether the RBP Proposal as filed—not as 
subsequently explained or refined—satisfies PJM’s section 205 burden. 
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE LIMITED ANSWER 
Although Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits answers to protests or answers absent 
Commission authorization, the Commission accepts otherwise-prohibited answers when they 
provide information that assists its decision-making,6 and clarify the record.7 Good cause exists 
here to justify the Commission’s granting this motion and accepting this Limited Answer. PJM’s 
Answer misconstrues or does not address central issues raised in EKPC’s Protest and First Limited 
Answer,8 including whether RBP costs and transmission owner exit fees bear a meaningful 
relationship to cost causation, whether PJM treats Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”) entities 
and Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) self-supply load-serving entities (“LSEs”) comparably,

(supporting protests filed by transmission owners addressing PJM’s proposed Transmission Owner exit fee provisions 
of the RBP).

and whether the proposed credit and default provisions define, secure, and allocate the relevant 
exposures in a just and reasonable manner. PJM also supplies new explanations and proposed 
concessions concerning severance of the buyer-side LSE credit rate, the timing and calculation of 
collateral, Peak Market Activity, and default allocation.9 This Limited Answer responds only to 
those matters and to PJM’s post-filing implementation explanations, will not prejudice any party 
or delay the proceeding, and will assist the Commission in evaluating whether PJM has carried its 
burden under section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”). The Commission should therefore 
accept this Limited Answer. 
II. 
BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY 
On July 31, 2026, PJM filed proposed revisions to its Tariff and RAA to establish a RBP 
intended to address identified capacity shortfalls associated with forecast large-load growth. 
EKPC’s Protest explained that a legitimate reliability objective does not excuse a rate design that 
fails to make costs, credits, collateral obligations, and default risks transparent, traceable, 
administrable, and reasonably tied to the entities that caused or benefit from the procurement.10 
PJM’s proposed fallback allocation still spreads RBP costs to load without demonstrating that the 
charged LSEs caused the procurement need or receive commensurate benefits. Its disparate 
treatment of FRR entities and RPM self-supply LSEs remains unexplained. And severing one 
credit-rate input leaves unresolved the nature, timing, quantity, release, and default treatment of 
the exposure being collateralized.  
PJM’s Answer does not cure those defects, and the allocation of the burden of proof 
matters. This is PJM’s section 205 filing. PJM therefore must establish, by record evidence and

10 See EKPC Protest at 11.

reasoned explanation, that the particular tariff rules it filed—not merely the reliability objective 
they pursue—are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.11 EKPC need 
not design a superior replacement or disprove every possible justification that PJM might have 
supplied. If PJM has not shown how its allocation, offset, collateral, and default provisions produce 
lawful outcomes, the statutory prerequisite to the Commission’s acceptance of the RBP Proposal 
is absent. The Commission therefore should reject the RBP Proposal or, at minimum, reject or set 
for further procedures the unsupported provisions identified below.12 
PJM’s evolving explanation of the buyer-side credit framework confirms that material 
aspects of the RBP Proposal remained under development after the PJM RBP Filing. PJM now 
offers to remove Tariff language concerning Peak Market Activity, clarifies that collateral is not 
due until 45 days before the first Delivery Year for which an LSE is responsible for RBP Charges, 
and consents to further procedures on the buyer-side credit rate.13 Whatever authority PJM has to 
make a section 205 filing, the relevant point is that the credit design now being defended was not 
fully presented in the stakeholder process or, most importantly for purposes of the Commission’s 
deliberation, in the filed tariff language presented in PJM’s RBP Filing. LSEs were asked to 
evaluate a proposal whose collateral mechanics, interaction with Peak Market Activity, timing, and 
exposure methodology were still being refined after protests were filed. That procedural history

III. 
LIMITED ANSWER 
A. PJM Has Not Carried Its Affirmative Burden Under FPA Section 205. 
Section 205 places the burden squarely on PJM to show that the RBP is just and reasonable. 
All jurisdictional rates and all rules and practices affecting them must be just and reasonable and 
not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and when a public utility proposes a change, “the burden 
of proof to show that the increased rate or charge is just and reasonable shall be upon the public 
utility.”14 The Commission’s regulations accordingly require a filing utility to submit the 
information necessary to explain and support the proposed change.15 The distinction from section 
206 of the FPA is fundamental: PJM is not defending an existing rate presumed lawful against an 
EKPC complaint; PJM is asking the Commission to authorize new tariff provisions.16 PJM itself 
has publicly described the governing rule the same way: a public utility making a section 205 filing 
“has the legal burden of demonstrating” that its proposed change is just and reasonable.17  
To satisfy this burden requires more than showing that a reliability problem exists or that 
PJM’s preferred mechanism is administratively convenient. PJM must connect the evidence to the 
specific rate design for which it seeks approval. And the Commission must evaluate the proposal 
actually filed on the record before it, provide a reasoned explanation for its conclusion, and respond 
 
14 16 U.S.C. § 824d(a), (b), (e). 
15 See 18 C.F.R. §§ 35.12, 35.13 (2026)  (any public utility filing a rate change must submit detailed data and statements 
to “sustain the burden of proof under the Federal Power Act of establishing that the rate increase is just and 
reasonable”). 
16 See City of Winnfield, 744 F.2d at 875. 
17 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Federal Law Guides Changes in PJM Governing Documents 1 (2025), available at: 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/fact-sheets/federal-power-act-sections-205-and-
206.pdf.

6 
 
to material objections that cast doubt on the proposal’s lawfulness.18 The Commission therefore 
cannot presume answers that PJM did not supply, rely on conclusory assertions that the proposal 
is “tailored,”19 or treat unanswered cost-causation questions as EKPC’s failure of proof. A material 
evidentiary gap is PJM’s failure to carry its section 205 burden. 
B. PJM Failed to Address EKPC’s Cost Causation Arguments.  
Cost causation is not a subsidiary policy preference that the Commission may bypass once 
PJM identifies a regional shortfall. A rate must reflect, at least to some degree, the costs caused by 
the customers required to pay it, and an allocation based on benefits must be at least roughly 
commensurate with the benefits received.20 PJM’s own Answer invokes the same principle: costs 
should be recovered from customers that use the facilities and cause the costs to be incurred.21 But 
PJM does not carry that principle through the RBP Proposal. 
PJM’s transmittal letter establishes a regional capacity shortfall and attributes much of the 
forecast growth to large loads.22 But PJM does not demonstrate each link necessary to justify the 
proposed charge. PJM does not identify how the forecast increment used to set the procurement 
target will be traced to the particular LSEs ultimately assessed RBP Charges, show that an Electric 
Distributor or state/Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”) allocation will 
preserve that causal link, require an offset or prudent existing supply to follow the LSE or load

Trade LLC v. FERC, 665 F.3d 203, 208 (D.C. Cir. 2011).

as “appropriately tailored”), 74 (the buyer-sider credit requirements are “appropriately tailored”).

that provided it, explain why a Peak Load Contribution-based (“PLC”) fallback measures 
causation by the identified large-load growth, or establish that a customer charged under the 
fallback measure will receive a benefit roughly commensurate with its assigned costs. Moreover, 
PJM’s proposed Tariff text likewise supplies no objective standard that answers those questions. 
Describing the mechanics of a downstream allocation process is not evidence that the resulting 
allocation is just and reasonable.23 
These are not isolated objections. Mr. Bednarczyk explained that the RBP fails to maintain 
a traceable link among incremental large-load responsibility, recognized mitigation, RBP 
Obligations (“RBO”) MW, RBP Charges, and collateral obligations.24 Mr. Coscia then showed that 
the credit construct compounds that defect because the collateral obligation is not derived from a 
measured exposure, is not tied to the timing of actual RBP settlement risk, and may itself create 
liquidity and default risk.25 PJM’s Answer addresses pieces of those critiques but does not supply 
the missing tariff standards needed to make the RBP framework administrable and causation-
based. 
PJM cannot cure the deficiencies by assigning the missing analysis to Electric Distributors, 
states, or RERRAs.26 Those entities may administer retail matters or choose how a valid wholesale 
obligation is recovered, but their later choices cannot supply the predicate showing PJM had to 
make when it filed the wholesale rate.27 If PJM’s Tariff does not provide a causation-based

allocation rule, a state’s later decision cannot retroactively make the filed wholesale rate just and 
reasonable. 
Nor may PJM’s Answer substitute new explanation for missing Tariff content. The 
Commission evaluates the filed rate as proposed, and regulated entities must be able to determine 
their obligations from the governing tariff rather than from post-filing assurances.28 Where PJM 
now offers clarifications, concessions, or severance to answer protests, those responses confirm 
that the as-filed provisions did not themselves resolve material uncertainties and issues of the 
proposed rated. 
Finally, the Commission may not save the RBP Filing by assembling a different proposal 
from stakeholder alternatives or by supplying its own reasoning to reinterpret filed tariff revisions 
that PJM did not provide.29 The stakeholder-supported subscription alternative referenced by 
EKPC in its Protest is relevant because it demonstrates that causation-based approaches existed, 
not because EKPC bears a burden to prove that alternative uniquely just and reasonable.30 EKPC 
further observes that PJM’s RBP Proposal inappropriately relies on downstream state/RERRA 
action. PJM could have adopted the stakeholder-supported proposal that relied on RERRA action 
at the outset of the backstop procurement process to ensure that LSEs serving Large Loads would

subscription. PJM’s concern with the stakeholder-supported proposal is that the PJM Board did 
not have confidence it addressed the capacity shortfall. However, reliance on states/RERRAs could 
have addressed the capacity shortfall concern while also affording certainty as to which LSEs 
would be receiving RBP allocations and be fully responsible for RBP costs and credit 
responsibilities and being consistent with cost-causation principles. More importantly, reliance on 
states/RERRAs at the start of a backstop procurement process would be consistent with 
establishing a valid wholesale obligation that would appropriately align with the state’s/RERRA’s 
responsibilities for retail rate determinations. 
C. EKPC’s Protest Is Consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. 
PJM suggests that EKPC’s execution of the Ratepayer Protection Pledge is inconsistent 
with its opposition to the RBP.31 The opposite is true. EKPC supports the principle that new large 
loads should build, bring, or buy the resources needed to serve their demands and bear the full 
associated costs. In fact, EKPC supported the Joint EDC & Data Center Coalition Reliability 
Backstop Procurement Proposal, which would have enabled states/RERRAs to act at the outset of 
an RBP process to ensure LSEs responsible to provide retail service to Large Loads subscribed to 
the procurement process so the appropriate amount of capacity is procured.  As noted above, this 
would have provided greater certainty, better aligned cost causation, and provided ratepayer 
protection by ensuring the appropriate LSEs are charged the costs they were directly responsible 
for incurring. EKPC protested the RBP because, as proposed, the RBP may shift those costs to 
LSEs and customers that prudently planned their portfolios and did not cause the residual

procurement need.32 A mechanism that can impose RBP charges, collateral burdens, or mutualized 
default exposure on non-causers conflicts with—rather than implements—the Pledge’s ratepayer-
protection objective.33 
PJM’s assertion that EKPC presently receives no direct RBP allocation does not answer 
EKPC’s fundamental objections to the RBP proposal.34 EKPC challenges the RBP Proposal, 
including its precedential and future effects, not merely its first illustrative assignment. 
Although PJM describes the RBP as a one-time process,35 the proposed Tariff and RAA language 
does not itself supply a clear one-time limitation, and PJM has publicly contemplated RBP or 
similar mechanisms in future reliability frameworks.36 The Commission must evaluate the filed 
provisions as proposed. 
PJM’s reliance on the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to support its transmission-owner exit 
provisions is similarly misplaced.37 Requiring entities that did not cause the RBP need to bear costs 
associated with pseudo-tying generation back into PJM after a transmission owner exits would

D. PJM Does Not Justify Disparate Treatment of FRR Entities and RPM Self 
Supply LSEs. 
 
PJM fundamentally misunderstands EKPC’s argument with respect to treatment of FRR 
entities. Contrary to PJM’s assertion, EKPC does not argue that FRR entities should be subjected 
to the RBP.39 EKPC’s point is comparability.40 PJM recognizes an FRR entity’s existing portfolio 
and excludes its load and supply from RBP exposure, while an RPM self-supply LSE may receive 
no comparable recognition for resources it already owns or procured to serve its customers.41 Both 
entities may have taken materially similar planning actions to satisfy aggregate resource 
obligations. PJM does not identify a relevant operational or cost-causation distinction that justifies 
insulating one portfolio while disregarding the other. 
That unexplained asymmetry raises classic undue-discrimination concerns. FPA section 
205(b) prohibits an undue preference or advantage and any unreasonable difference in rates or 
service among similarly situated customers.42 That FRR entities face a deficiency rate does not 
cure the problem, particularly where that rate is not yet effective for the relevant period.43 Nor 
does moving related FRR language to the IRAS docket establish that the RBP’s differential

E. PJM’s Proposed Credit-Rate Severance Does Not Cure the RBP’s Credit 
and Default Defects. 
 
As detailed in the EKPC Protest, PJM’s proposed collateral requirements are unjust and 
unreasonable and should be rejected.45 If the Commission nevertheless accepts PJM’s proposal to 
sever the buyer-side LSE credit rate for further procedures, the numerical rate is only one 
component of the defect.46 Any further proceeding must define the exposure being secured, the 
quantity to which the rate applies, the date on which the obligation arises, objective reduction and 
release standards, the interaction with Operating Agreement section 15.2.2, and the liquidity and 
default consequences created by the requirement. Severing one input cannot make the remainder 
of the RBP just and reasonable when the obligation’s basic operation remains uncertain. 
PJM’s Answer also contains unresolved inconsistencies. PJM states that EKPC would 
receive no RBP cost allocation or reallocation under proposed section 18.9(a), yet PJM invokes 
Operating Agreement section 15.2.2—and the need to protect PJM Members from LSE default—
to justify the collateral requirement.47 If section 18.9 fully contains an RBP default within the pool 
of LSEs assigned RBP Charges, PJM should state that limitation in the governing Tariff text. If 
residual unpaid amounts may reach all PJM Members under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2, 
then EKPC’s lack of a direct RBP allocation does not eliminate its exposure. PJM cannot rely on

PJM’s remaining clarifications likewise do not conform to the filed Tariff. First, PJM offers 
to delete the sentence stating that RBP settlement may be included in Peak Market Activity,48 but 
does not explain how an invoiced RBP billing item is excluded from Peak Market Activity or 
whether Attachment Q requires a conforming revision. Second, PJM states that no LSE collateral 
is required until an RBP Resource is in service for the applicable Delivery Year,49 but proposed 
section 18.8(b)(i)(A)—the buyer-side cumulative requirement—defines committed RBP UCAP 
MW without an express in-service limitation. Third, PJM states that collateral is based on 
committed MW,50 while section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) scales the LSE posting to the Final RBP Target. 
If procurement clears below that target, the filed language does not specify which quantity controls 
aggregate collateral.

year transition study to fifteen years and reports an approximately 11 percent probability that a 
BBB obligor reaches default and 36.9 percent for a BB obligor.51 But that table measures migration 
arising in the ordinary course; it does not measure what happens to an LSE’s financial condition 
when PJM imposes a collateral obligation of the magnitude proposed here.52 On PJM’s own 
allocation, the cooperative with the second-largest zonal assignment would post approximately 
114 percent of its total assets, roughly twice its equity, and about eight times its cash, while a 100-

existed, including that buyer-side credit could be managed through existing processes. 56 The June

procurement registry identifying which LSEs must support collateral and for how many 
megawatts, with a gate preventing procurement for load whose responsible LSE or large-load 
customer could not post.57 PJM states that the filed LSE credit requirement has roots in the Joint 
EDC/ Data Center Coalition proposal,58 but the filed design adopts the assignment to LSEs without 
the registry, gate, or exposure-funding mechanics that tied credit responsibility to the load being 
procured for. This record reinforces that causation-based approaches existed on the precise credit

default exposure is recognized early, funded continuously, and contained entirely within 
the buyer over time.” That package was the only one of the thirteen voted at the close of 
Stage 4 to receive greater than two-thirds sector-weighted member support. It identified 
the obligated entity and its megawatt quantity before the procurement, conditioned the 
procurement on the ability to post, and measured exposure as it emerged.

8 
 
35. The July 31 filing established a separate RBP Credit Requirement at a Credit Rate of $1.5 
million per MW, a figure that appears in none of the stakeholder materials I have reviewed. 
PJM states that the Board “adopted various concepts from the Coalition RBP Proposal that 
received a sector-weighted majority of stakeholder support,” and identifies the “credit 
requirement for Load Serving Entities” as among those with “roots in the Coalition RBP 
Proposal.” July 31 Filing at 22. The filed construct incorporates the assignment of the 
obligation to LSEs. It does not incorporate the registry, the identification of the obligated 
entity before the procurement, the requirement to post before the obligation attaches, or the 
continuous funding of exposure as it emerges. 
36. Opinion. PJM is not obliged to adopt a stakeholder proposal, and it may reasonably have 
concluded that Peak Market Activity alone was insufficient for a fifteen-year obligation. 
What the Answer supplies is an explanation of why PJM now considers Peak Market 
Activity inadequate. What it does not supply is the analytical bridge from the approaches 
PJM had before it, its own March exposure modeling, the existing credit processes it 
proposed through June 30, and the Coalition’s exposure-based design, to a rate initially 
approximating one-half of the gross fifteen-year payment stream. 
V. 
THE QUANTITY ON WHICH COLLATERAL IS REQUIRED IS NOT DEFINED 
37. An LSE cannot calculate its posting unless the tariff identifies the controlling megawatt 
quantity. Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.8(b)(i)(A) requires collateral equal 
to the RBP Credit Rate multiplied by “RBP UCAP MW committed.” The amount of the 
requirement therefore depends entirely on that quantity. PJM’s Answer and its 
implementation materials leave three questions about it unresolved: whether the megawatts 
must be in service; whether an individual LSE’s posting follows the megawatts its Electric 
Distributor assigns or is scaled to the Final RBP Target; and what quantity applies, if any, 
where the Electric Distributor reports nothing. 
A. Whether the megawatts must be in service 
38. PJM’s Answer states that “no collateral would be required for RBP Resources [that] are 
not in service for that Delivery Year.” PJM Answer at 78 n.234. 
39. That in-service limitation does not appear in section 18.8(b)(i)(A). That provision defines 
the quantity as “the amount of RBP UCAP MW that receives a commitment through the 
Reliability Backstop Procurement minus each commitment of RBP UCAP MW that is 
rescinded pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.6(e).” Commitments received, 
less rescissions. There is no in-service condition, and PJM has proposed no revision to that 
provision. 
40. Rescission under section 18.6(e) occurs only “where RBP UCAP MW fail to come online 
for three Delivery Years beginning with the first Delivery Year in which the RBP Resource 
was committed.” A resource that has not achieved commercial operation therefore remains 
within the quantity for up to three Delivery Years. PJM’s transmittal describes the same 
mechanic and identifies rescission as the operative event: the input “will change as 
committed resources fail to follow through on their commitment and do not achieve 
commercial operation,” and it is the rescinded commitment that “is subtracted from the 
input used to determine the uniform RBP credit requirement.” July 31 Filing at 116.

9 
 
41. The September 14 Presentation states the Answer’s position on one slide and applies the 
tariff definition on another. Slide 9 defines the quantity as “the level of RBP UCAP MW 
for which an LSE is allocated cost responsibility submitted for the buyer by the EDC,” and 
adds in a note that “Committed MW is equal to the generation that is coming online for 
that delivery year.” 
42. Example #4 at slide 57 of the September 14 Presentation does the opposite. It addresses a 
unit that “does not come online for Delivery Year.” The example carries Committed MW 
(UCAP) of 50 throughout, assesses the RBP Shortfall Charge on all 50 committed 
megawatts under section 18.6(d), and computes RBP Credits on Daily Owned MW of zero. 
The commitment remains at 50 megawatts and settlement occurs on that quantity even 
though the resource is not in service. That is the filed definition, applied. 
43. The two formulas use different quantities. RBP Credits, and therefore the RBP Charges 
assessed to load, are computed on Daily Owned MW, which is why the charge is zero in 
Example #4. The collateral requirement in section 18.8(b)(i)(A) is computed on RBP 
UCAP MW committed, which in the same example remains 50. The absence of a charge 
in a Delivery Year is a result of the credit formula. It does not change the quantity to which 
the Credit Rate applies. 
B. Whether the posting follows assigned megawatts or the Final RBP Target 
44. Section 18.8(b)(i)(A) sets the cumulative RBP credit requirement for all LSEs as the Credit 
Rate multiplied by committed megawatts. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) sets each individual 
LSE’s posting as $1.5 million multiplied by the RBP Obligation MW its Electric 
Distributor submits, “scaled, as necessary, in the event that the RBP Obligation MW values 
uploaded by the Electric Distributor do not sum to the fixed, Final RBP Target MW for the 
zone/area.” 
45. Those provisions use different quantities, and PJM states the procurement may clear short 
of the Final RBP Target. Where it does, committed megawatts are fewer than the Target. 
The individual postings scaled to the Target under (B)(1) would then sum to more than the 
cumulative requirement calculated on committed megawatts under (A). Because the Credit 
Rate is $1.5 million per megawatt, each 100 megawatts of difference between the two 
quantities changes the aggregate amount posted by $150 million. 
46. PJM has identified each quantity as governing. Footnote 234 states that the amount “would 
be based on the RBP UCAP MW committed for that Delivery Year.” PJM’s written 
response of August 14, 2026 stated that the Final RBP Target governs. 
C. What applies where the Electric Distributor reports nothing 
47. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) provides that where no RBP Obligations are reported for an 
Electric Distributor zone or area, LSEs serving load there “may be required to post” 
collateral calculated on “the [LSE’s] pro-rata share of the Daily Unforced Capacity 
Obligation for the zone/area as determined in RAA, Schedule 8.” The September 14 
Presentation states that measure at slide 70, while a footnote to the example at slide 69 
describes the same fallback as a Peak Load Contribution allocation. 
48. The provision is permissive, and PJM confirmed in writing on September 15, 2026 that it 
admits more than one outcome. An LSE may be required to post at the Credit Rate, may 
post at the Credit Rate and additionally be assessed under the Unreasonable Credit Risk

10 
 
provisions of Attachment Q, Section II, or may not be required to post at the Credit Rate 
but be subject to an unreasonable credit risk assessment. The provision states that an LSE 
“may be required to post.” It does not state that a Credit Rate posting is required in every 
case in which no RBP Obligations are reported. 
49. The quantity also changes basis. Under (B)(1) an LSE posts on megawatts attributed to it 
through the allocation process. Under (B)(2) it posts on its share of total load. An entity 
with no RBP Obligation under section 18.3 has no requirement under (B)(1) and a 
requirement measured by its entire load under (B)(2). 
50. Subsection (B)(2) is also difficult to square with PJM’s defense of the uniform rate. PJM 
states that its methodology “is based on the committed obligation itself and avoids having 
the adequacy of the credit protection depend upon long-range predictions about individual 
LSE’s financials.” PJM Answer at 82. The Unreasonable Credit Risk provisions of 
Attachment Q, Section II are an individualized assessment of a participant’s financial 
condition. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(2) routes directly into them, and PJM has confirmed that 
an assessment may be made in place of, or in addition to, a Credit Rate posting. PJM has 
therefore built individualized credit evaluation into the construct. It applies where an 
Electric Distributor fails to report, and not where the Electric Distributor reports. 
D. Timing 
51. Section 18.3(b)(iii) requires the initial allocation to be reported no later than sixty days 
before the Delivery Year, and collateral is due prior to forty-five days before. An LSE 
would have approximately fifteen days between learning which subsection applies to it, 
and on what quantity, and funding the requirement. 
52. The timing differs from the forward-exposure rationale. PJM relies on the long-dated 
character of the obligation to distinguish it from Peak Market Activity, while requiring no 
security until shortly before the first applicable Delivery Year. The near-term exposure is 
determined well before then. 
53. Both of the first two Delivery Years are subject to the price collar PJM extended through 
2029/2030. The collar is expressed in installed capacity terms and converted to unforced 
capacity by the Effective Load Carrying Capability rating of the reference resource. The 
2028/2029 Base Residual Auction cleared at the collared cap of $325.00/MW-day UCAP 
at a Gas CT Dual Fuel rating of 79 percent, and the 2027/2028 auction cleared at its collared 
cap of $333.44/MW-day at a rating of 77 percent. Both imply the same basis of 
$256.75/MW-day ICAP. PJM endorsed a Gas CT Dual Fuel rating of 76 percent for 
2029/2030 on August 19, 2026, which places the collared cap for that Delivery Year at 
$337.83/MW-day UCAP and the floor at $181.91/MW-day UCAP. 
54. At the $555.00/MW-day maximum willingness to pay, the differential is therefore 
$230.00/MW-day for 2028/2029 and $217.17/MW-day for 2029/2030, or $83,950 and 
$79,267 per MW respectively. The two-year total is $163,217 per MW, which on an 
adjusted target of approximately 6,000 MW is approximately $979 million, and 
approximately $1.115 billion on the full Initial RBP Target of 6,831.3 MW. These figures 
replace the $333.44 proxy I used at paragraph 92 of my original affidavit, the 2029/2030 
parameters not having been endorsed when that affidavit was prepared. The amount is

11 
 
determined once the 2029/2030 auction clears in December 2026, and no collateral is 
required against it until approximately April 17, 2028. 
55. Opinion. An LSE cannot determine from the filed rate the quantity on which it must post. 
The tariff, the Answer, and the implementation presentation give different answers to 
whether the megawatts must be in service, and PJM’s own settlement example applies the 
tariff definition rather than the Answer’s. PJM has identified both committed megawatts 
and the Final RBP Target as governing an individual posting. And where an Electric 
Distributor reports nothing, whether an entity posts at all, on what quantity, and whether it 
is additionally assessed for unreasonable credit risk are matters the filed provisions leave 
to discretion. If PJM intends collateral to follow in-service megawatts, or the Final RBP 
Target, those are changes to section 18.8(b)(i) and should be made in the tariff. 
VI. THE EXPOSURE THE REQUIREMENT SECURES IS LARGELY ORDINARY 
RPM ACTIVITY 
A. Coordination with Attachment Q 
56. PJM proposes to delete the sentence providing that settlement of cleared RBP positions 
“may be included, as appropriate, in Peak Market Activity,” on the basis that it could cause 
confusion that RBP Charges may be captured in that calculation. 
57. Removal of the clause does not establish how an invoiced RBP billing line item is excluded 
from the Peak Market Activity calculation in Attachment Q, section VII.A, and PJM has 
proposed no conforming revision to Attachment Q. Three provisions are unaffected by the 
deletion and bear on the coordination question. Nothing in section 18 supersedes 
Attachment Q. The RBP requirements are separate from and additional to credit 
requirements arising under Attachment Q. And under sections 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) and (B)(2), 
PJM may evaluate an LSE for unreasonable credit risk under Attachment Q, Section II and 
require additional RBP Collateral, which as set out at paragraph 47 above may be done in 
addition to, or in place of, a Credit Rate posting. 
58. PJM explains the separate requirement as securing the forward RPM component of the 
obligation together with the contract-for-differences amount, on the ground that Peak 
Market Activity does not prospectively collateralize the RPM component over the term. 
The RBP settles economically through RPM and a contract-for-differences: load pays the 
RPM clearing price through ordinary capacity billing and pays or receives the difference 
through the new billing line item. 
59. To examine how that explanation operates, I apply it to a period in which three Delivery 
Years remain, at an RBP commitment price of $555.00/MW-day on 6,000 MW. I take a 
Base Residual Auction clearing price of $554.00/MW-day, at which the contract-for-
differences is nearly extinguished. The result is set out in Table 1.

60. The discontinuity is in the treatment of the RPM component. At an RPM clearing price of 
$554.00, an LSE carrying an ordinary capacity obligation of that size would be subject to 
PJM’s ordinary Attachment Q credit processes. The same entity carrying the same RPM 
obligation, plus a contract-for-differences of $1.00/MW-day, has that RPM stream treated 
as part of a multi-year forward obligation supporting a separate collateral requirement. An 
incremental obligation of $2.19 million a year changes the credit treatment of 
approximately $1.2 billion a year of ordinary RPM payments. 
61. Opinion. PJM has not explained why the existence of an RBP commitment changes the 
credit treatment of the forward RPM payment stream, or how that separate treatment should 
converge with ordinary RPM credit treatment as the contract-for-differences amount and 
the remaining term decline. 
VII. PJM’S ILLUSTRATION OF THE REDUCTION PROVISION 
62. I addressed the absence of a defined reduction and release standard at opinion 7(f) and 
paragraphs 47 and 155 of my original affidavit, including the comparison with Attachment 
Q, Section V.A and Section VI.B.3 and with the seller-side release in section 18.8(a). I do 
not repeat that analysis. PJM has since explained how the provision is intended to operate, 
and I address that explanation. 
63. PJM states in its Answer that the Credit Rate can decline where previously required 
collateral exceeds the remaining expected payment exposure, and acknowledges that use 
of the actual weighted-average RBP price may be appropriate. PJM Answer at 80 & n.240. 
64. The September 14 Presentation illustrates the result. Slide 69 sets out a roll-off schedule 
for a 100 MW RBP Obligation at the $1.5 million Credit Rate, assuming a $555.00/MW-
day commitment price, an annual payment obligation of $20,257,500, and no change to 
committed megawatts over the fifteen-year term. Collateral of $150,000,000 is held 
without change for the first eight Delivery Years. The first reduction occurs in 2036/2037, 
the ninth Delivery Year, and PJM explains it in a note: “Credit requirement/collateral is 
reduced due to payment obligation is smaller than collateral held.” The requirement then 
tracks the remaining gross payment obligation to $20,257,500 in the final year. 
65. The requirement does not decline for more than half the term. Over the first eight Delivery 
Years the remaining gross payment obligation falls from $303,862,500 to $162,060,000, a 
reduction of approximately forty-seven percent, while the collateral held remains at

13 
 
$150,000,000. PJM has separately modeled exposure on this construct. In the March 4 
Credit Overview at 12 it modeled the procurement as a fixed-for-float swap and produced 
a potential future exposure profile that begins at zero, rises through the early Delivery 
Years, reaches a maximum within roughly the first third of the term, and declines to zero 
at expiry, stating that “[t]he value uncertainty goes higher deeper into the future, while 
quantity exposure decreases as time goes by. This makes PFE peaks at 1/3 of life.” Potential 
future exposure and remaining gross payments are different measures, and I do not suggest 
the schedule should replicate the March profile. What PJM has not explained is why the 
buyer-side requirement follows remaining gross payments rather than a profile sensitive to 
the exposure it is said to secure, when PJM has modeled that exposure itself. 
66. The reduction, when it occurs, tracks the remaining gross payment obligation rather than 
the exposure. The schedule is built from the $555.00/MW-day commitment price applied 
to full committed megawatts; the annual figure of $20,257,500 is that price multiplied by 
365 days and 100 MW. It contains no RPM clearing price and therefore no contract-for-
differences input. 
67. The schedule is an illustration rather than a rule. It appears in a presentation, it assumes 
committed megawatts do not change over the term, and nothing in section 18.8(b)(i)(A) 
requires PJM to follow it or establishes its frequency or inputs. 
68. Opinion. PJM’s illustration shows collateral held flat for eight of fifteen Delivery Years 
and reducing thereafter on the remaining gross payment obligation, on an assumption the 
tariff does not require, under a provision that is permissive throughout. The illustrated 
requirement therefore does not respond to the contract-for-differences amount or observed 
RPM clearing prices, and it does not decline with remaining tenor during the first eight 
Delivery Years. 
VIII. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR ADDITIONAL PROCEEDINGS 
69. PJM has consented to the Commission resolving the buyer-side Credit Rate through 
additional procedures, and states that the buyer-side rules need not be effective for the 
Reliability Backstop Procurement to be conducted. The matters set out below should be 
resolved on a schedule that reflects when the underlying exposure becomes measurable, 
which, as set out in paragraph 5, is well before the filed posting date. 
70. In my opinion, any additional procedures should define the exposure the requirement is 
intended to secure and the quantity and timing of that exposure before a replacement Credit 
Rate is selected. That includes the relationship among the RPM component of the payment, 
the contract-for-differences amount created by the RBP, the reallocation provided by 
section 18.9(a), and any residual exposure under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2. It 
also requires a defined meaning of “RBP UCAP MW committed” and its relationship to 
megawatts in service, megawatts allocated to an LSE, RBP Obligation MW reported by an 
Electric Distributor, and the Final RBP Target. The procedures should also establish when 
the resulting exposure arises and when collateral is required in relation to it. 
71. The methodology should then provide objective standards for recalculating and releasing 
collateral as the relevant conditions change, including the RBP commitment price, 
observed RPM clearing prices and resulting contract-for-differences amounts, remaining 
tenor, committed quantity, and participant credit condition. It should also establish the

14 
 
order in which collateral, the reallocation under section 18.9(a), and any mutualization 
under Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 apply, so that the residual loss the collateral is 
intended to secure can be identified. 
72. PJM’s Answer and implementation materials supply explanations that were not available 
when I submitted my original affidavit. They do not establish the relationship between the 
collateral required and the exposure secured. 
73. The question presented by the buyer-side credit requirement is therefore not whether $1.5 
million per MW is too high or too low. It is whether the amount, the quantity, the timing, 
the recalculation, the release, and the default treatment of collateral bear a defined 
relationship to the exposure the requirement is intended to secure. On the present record 
they do not. 
74. This concludes my reply affidavit.
